verified citation: Gulley SP, Rasch EK, Chan L. Ongoing coverage for ongoing care: access, utilization, and out-of-pocket spending among uninsured working-aged adults with chronic health care needs. Am J Public Health. 2011;101(2):368-375. doi:10.2105/AJPH.2010.191569. PMID 21164090; PMCID PMC3020213.
accessible source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3020213/ (PMC full text read, including Results text and Table 2)
actual task/data: MEPS-HC 2002-2004 pooled annual files linked to the Medical Conditions and event files (n=58,408 adults aged 18-64; weighted average-annual estimates). Chronic conditions came from ICD codes on a validated list of conditions expected to last at least 12 months, split by disability status (none; disability not affecting ADL/IADL; disability affecting ADL/IADL). Coverage came from MEPS monthly indicators, summarized as insured all year / uninsured 1-5 months / 6-11 months / all 12 months. Outcomes were delayed or forgone medical care and prescriptions, mean ambulatory visits, mean annual prescription fills, and family out-of-pocket spending (premiums excluded) of at least 15% of family income.
methods: Cross-sectional, design-based descriptive and regression analysis: weighted means and percentages with Taylor-series variance; pairwise t-tests with false discovery rate control; logistic models for access outcomes and two-part GEE log-link models for utilization.
limitation relevant here: Data predate the ACA (2002-2004). The chronic-condition group is broad, with no diabetes-specific estimate. Coverage groups are defined by duration of uninsurance only and are never cross-classified with December 31 status, so the paper cannot say how many people a year-end indicator would label insured. The transition split it reports (about 40% of part-year uninsured lost coverage and did not regain it by year end, about 40% gained coverage and kept it through year end, about 20% moved both into and out of coverage) applies to all adults 18-64, not to the chronic-condition group, and the year-end status of the 20% with multiple transitions is not given. The out-of-pocket outcome is a family income-burden threshold, not prescription out-of-pocket dollars. Associations only.
overlap with this project: Same survey, same age band and the same monthly coverage source, with continuity categories close to the project's monthly classification. Among adults with a chronic condition it reports mean annual prescription fills of 18.17 (SE 0.28) for those insured all year, 12.63 (0.52) for 1-5 uninsured months, 11.88 (0.59) for 6-11 months and 10.17 (0.40) for all 12 months. For the same groups, out-of-pocket burden of at least 15% of income was 4.52%, 6.78%, 12.62% and 16.60%, and delayed or forgone prescriptions 5.84%, 10.12%, 18.81% and 14.00%. Overall, 21% of adults with chronic conditions were uninsured at least 1 month (about 10 million all year and about 10 million part-year). The gained-and-kept group is the population that a year-end indicator classifies as insured.
what this project adds: Restricts to adults with diabetes who were insured on 12/31 (DIABDX_M18=1, INS24X=1) and estimates the weighted share with at least one fully uninsured month, which in practice falls in January-November. Uses 2024 data (after the ACA and the Medicaid unwinding). Reports person-level prescription out-of-pocket dollars (RXSLF24) and fills (RXTOT24) under the year-end and the monthly representation side by side, rather than by continuity alone. Releases a reusable classifier with an explicit indeterminate class for out-of-scope months.

verified citation: Keenan PS, Vistnes J. Non-Elderly Adults Ever Uninsured During the Calendar Year, 2013-2016. Research Findings #42. Rockville, MD: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality; June 2019. Accessed October 7, 2026. https://meps.ahrq.gov/data_files/publications/rf42/rf42.pdf (read together with its companion report: Vistnes J, Keenan P. Uninsured All Year, 2013-2016. Research Findings #40. AHRQ; January 2019. https://meps.ahrq.gov/data_files/publications/rf40/rf40.pdf)
accessible source: https://meps.ahrq.gov/data_files/publications/rf42/rf42.pdf (official AHRQ PDF, full text read; HTTP 200 on 2026-10-07); companion https://meps.ahrq.gov/data_files/publications/rf40/rf40.pdf
actual task/data: MEPS-HC Full Year Consolidated files HC-163, HC-171, HC-181 and HC-192 (2013-2016) with state of residence added. Sample: adults aged 18-64 throughout the year and in scope all 12 months, excluding people who were institutionalized, left the country, died or joined after January. 'Ever uninsured' meant no coverage in at least 1 month, where a month counts as insured if coverage existed for any part of it (Medicaid, Medicare, TRICARE, other public hospital/physician programs, private hospital/physician or Marketplace). Noncomprehensive state programs and single-service plans count as uninsured. Chronic condition meant at least 1 of 9 conditions, including diabetes ('ever told'), active asthma, arthritis, emphysema, heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, bronchitis and stroke.
methods: Descriptive weighted percentages and population counts by demographics, health status, chronic-condition status and state Medicaid expansion status, with significance tested at p<0.05. RF #40 uses the same sample and definitions for the all-12-months uninsured measure.
limitation relevant here: Diabetes is pooled into a 9-condition group, with no diabetes-only estimate. The ever-uninsured measure is not conditioned on year-end status, so its part-year component mixes people who lost coverage and stayed uninsured through December 31 with people who gained or regained coverage before year end. Data are from 2013-2016. There are no prescription outcomes. Estimates appear in text and figures without standard errors in the text.
overlap with this project: Same file family, age band, full-year in-scope restriction and monthly any-coverage rule (a month counts as insured if covered any part of it), the same rule that defines a 'fully uninsured month' in HC-256. In 2016, 18.2% of adults with at least 1 chronic condition were ever uninsured versus 26.2% with none (22.0% of all adults 18-64). In RF #40, 7.8% of adults with a chronic condition were uninsured all year versus 14.0% with none (10.8% overall). Subtracting gives about 10.4 percentage points of part-year uninsurance among adults with chronic conditions (derived arithmetic, not an AHRQ-reported figure).
what this project adds: Isolates diabetes, conditions on insured status at 12/31 so that only the hidden part-year gaps are counted, updates to 2024, and links the classification to RXSLF24 and RXTOT24. The project can also state whether it keeps or relaxes the RF #42 full-year in-scope restriction, and report the effect of that choice.

verified citation: Wang Y, Park J, Li R, Luman E, Zhang P. National trends in out-of-pocket costs among U.S. adults with diabetes aged 18-64 years: 2001-2017. Diabetes Care. 2021;44(11):2510-2517. doi:10.2337/dc20-2833. PMID 34429323; PMCID PMC9578147.
actual task/data: MEPS-HC 2001-2017 repeated cross-sections, plus the MEPS Diabetes Care Survey for the insulin-use subgroup. Adults 18-64 answering yes to the 'ever told you had diabetes' question (n=22,649; 959-1,557 per year). Insurance: 'uninsured' meant no insurance in any month of the survey year. Everyone else was classed public or private by the type held longest, so people uninsured for part of the year sit inside the insured groups. Outcome: family-level out-of-pocket costs (premiums, prescription drugs, inpatient and outpatient cost sharing, uncovered payments) in 2017 dollars, broken down by service type, and a high-burden rate defined as family out-of-pocket costs above 10% of pretax family income.
methods: Joinpoint regression (up to 3 joinpoints, Monte Carlo permutation tests) and OLS linear trends, using SAS survey procedures with MEPS person weights (Diabetes Care Survey weights for the insulin subgroup). Two sensitivity analyses: excluding Medicare, and a second described in Methods as excluding people with more than one insurance type and in Results as limiting the public and private groups to full-year coverage.
limitation relevant here: Out-of-pocket costs are family-level and include premiums, unlike person-level RXSLF24. Only full-year uninsured people count as uninsured, and the paper never estimates how many people in the 'insured' groups had a gap. The full-year sensitivity analysis drops people with gaps rather than reclassifying them, and it reports only the high-burden rate. Data end in 2017.
overlap with this project: Same data source, age band and diabetes question, and it reports prescription out-of-pocket costs by insurance type. Total out-of-pocket costs fell from $4,328 to $4,139 (2001-2017). The high-burden rate fell from 28% to 19% in the abstract (18% in the Results text). Prescription out-of-pocket costs fell by $50.9 per year overall (P<0.0001), with the steepest decline among the uninsured (-$99 per year). Limiting the public and private groups to full-year coverage changed the high-burden rate by less than 1 percentage point and left the trends unchanged. This is the standard MEPS diabetes classification that the project contrasts with monthly continuity.
what this project adds: Counts year-end-insured adults with diabetes who had at least one fully uninsured month. Reports person-level RXSLF24 and RXTOT24 under the year-end and the monthly representation, rather than as a sensitivity exclusion. Uses 2024 data. Tests directly whether Wang et al.'s finding that gaps barely moved the high-burden rate also holds for prescription dollars and fills.

verified citation: Gai Y, Jones K. Insurance patterns and instability from 2006 to 2016. BMC Health Serv Res. 2020;20(1):334. doi:10.1186/s12913-020-05226-1. PMID 32316952; PMCID PMC7171789.
accessible source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7171789/ (CC BY; full-text XML read via E-utilities efetch db=pmc)
actual task/data: MEPS-HC longitudinal panels 11-20 (2006-2016), each a 2-year panel analyzed with longitudinal weights. Population: people under 65 with complete monthly insurance status. Tables say 'non-elderly adults (64 years and under)', but subgroup tables include ages 0-18. Coverage: monthly public/private/uninsured status over 24 months, classified into 7 patterns (always insured, single gap, transition into coverage, transition out of coverage, temporary coverage, repeatedly uninsured, always uninsured); source switches without a gap stay in the same pattern. Outcomes: 16 measures, including composite lack of access (no usual source of care, or unable to get or delayed medical care, dental care or prescription medicine) and 2-year utilization, including the number of prescribed medicines.
methods: Weighted distributions of the patterns by panel and by subgroup (age, income, region, race/ethnicity, AHRQ priority conditions including diabetes). Linear probability and OLS models with 'always insured' as the reference, adjusted for socioeconomic, demographic and health variables, priority conditions, panel and region. Logit, Poisson and log-linear robustness checks; Stata 15. The utilization models have n=3,706 against about 123,000 in the access models, and the paper does not explain the difference.
limitation relevant here: Uses a 24-month panel window rather than a calendar year. Patterns are never compared with a December 31 or other point-in-time indicator. Priority conditions are pooled, with no diabetes estimate. The prescription outcome is a count, not out-of-pocket dollars. The population appears to include children. The small, unexplained utilization sample limits the prescription results. Data are from before 2017. Associations only.
overlap with this project: The closest MEPS methodological analogue: monthly indicators turned into a continuity typology, framed explicitly as point-in-time measurement versus instability, with a prescription-use outcome. Any interruption (patterns 2-7) was 31.67% in 2006-07, peaked at 34.57% in 2008-09 and fell to 25.68% in 2015-16. Uninterrupted coverage among people with priority conditions rose from 65.95% to 74.67%. Mean uninsured months in the single-gap pattern were 4.10 in 2015-16. Compared with always insured, 2-year prescribed medicines were lower by 2.27 (single gap, p<0.10), 2.34 (transition into, p<0.05), 1.62 (transition out, p<0.05), 3.70 (temporary coverage), 3.74 (repeatedly uninsured) and 3.29 (always uninsured; last three p<0.01).
what this project adds: A single-calendar-year (2024) version of the typology anchored to 12/31 status, giving one class (insured at year end with at least one fully uninsured month) that combines Gai and Jones's single-gap, transition-into and repeated-gap patterns when they end insured. The project estimates that class directly for adults with diabetes, compares prescription out-of-pocket dollars and fills across the two representations, and releases the classification code.

GitHub; repository commit 02fbdd634959e97bd3584c3e9abdc62f84291d70 (June 9, 2026); Exercise 5b file commit a2514deccd563b14399e2745670d09ccd40eaf78 (August 14, 2019). Accessed October 7, 2026. https://github.com/HHS-AHRQ/MEPS
accessible source: https://github.com/HHS-AHRQ/MEPS; code read at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HHS-AHRQ/MEPS/master/SAS/workshop_exercises/exercise_5b/Exercise5b.sas, the matching Exercise5b_OUTPUT.TXT, Stata/workshop_exercises/Exercise5b.do, and R/summary_tables_examples/ins_age_2016.R
actual task/data: 2015 MEPS-HC Full Year Consolidated file (H181), all persons. The program loops over the 12 monthly any-insurance indicators INSJAyyX-INSDEyyX (1 = insured, 2 = uninsured, -1 = out of scope) and source-specific monthly arrays (PRI, MCD, MCR, TRI, PEG, PNG, PRX and others). It counts INS_N (insured months), UNINS_N (uninsured months) and REF_N (months with a positive code, labeled '# OF MONTHS IN MEPS SURVEY'). Flags: FULL_INSU=1 if UNINS_N=0; GROUP_INS1 (ever group coverage); GROUP_INS2 (group coverage in all in-scope months).
methods: Audit crosstabs (PROC FREQ FULL_INSU*UNINS_N and FULL_INSU*INS_N*REF_N; Stata tab), then design-based estimation with PROC SURVEYMEANS (STRATA VARSTR, CLUSTER VARPSU, WEIGHT PERWT15F, DOMAIN RACETHX) or Stata svy: mean. The R summary-table examples use survey::svydesign(id=~VARPSU, strata=~VARSTR, weights=~PERWTyyF, nest=TRUE) with options(survey.lonely.psu='adjust') and the annual INSCOV/INSURC classification. Output (2015): unweighted FULL_INSU=1 for 27,271 of 35,427 records; weighted mean FULL_INSU 0.822103 (SE 0.004876; sum of weights 321,423,251).
limitation relevant here: Does not use the December 31 indicator and has no 'insured at year end but at least one uninsured month' class. Counts only total uninsured months, with no spells or transitions. FULL_INSU=1 is assigned to anyone with zero uninsured months, including people with fewer than 12 in-scope months (REF_N<12) and records whose months are all -1, so out-of-scope months are not separated from covered months. The monthly construction exists only in SAS and Stata, is hard-coded to 2015 variable suffixes, and has no diabetes subgroup or prescription outcomes. The README states that AHRQ cannot certify the quality of users' analyses.
overlap with this project: Same monthly variables and coding, same month-counting logic (insured, uninsured and in-scope months), the same audit-crosstab check before estimation, and the same Taylor-linearization design (VARSTR, VARPSU, person weight). The R conventions (lonely PSU adjustment, subsetting the design object for domains) match the project's estimation approach.
what this project adds: An R classification function parameterized by year that keeps in-scope and out-of-scope (-1) months separate. It assigns mutually exclusive classes relative to 12/31 status: insured all in-scope months; insured at year end with at least one fully uninsured month; uninsured at year end; and indeterminate when out-of-scope months prevent classification. It outputs a weighted and unweighted audit table including INS24X by INSDE24X concordance, and is applied to adults 18-64 with DIABDX_M18=1 in HC-256 with RXSLF24 and RXTOT24 summaries.
